extracted.intended_audience: students, coaches, and organizers involved in math olympiads (USAMO/USAJMO/IMO/MOP)
extracted.subtask_description: A FAQ summarizing rules, selection procedures, grading rubrics, and practical guidance for math olympiad contests (USAMO, USAJMO, APMO, MOP, IMO) aimed at contestants, coaches, and interested parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: USA IMO team selection procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting in 2011 (as of 2019) — USA(J)MO, MOP, TSTST, TSTs, RMM/APMO/USAMO weightings and aggregation determine the IMO team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rough outline: ~250 students qualify for USAMO and ~250 for USA(J)MO via prior contests. From USAMO of year N-1, about 60 students (grades ≤11) and that year's IMO team are invited to MOP. At end of MOP a TSTST is given; top ~30 are selected for year-round TST’s for IMO of year N. Two TSTs (December & January) are each worth 21 points; RMM Day 1 is worth 21 points; APMO is weighted by 0.6 (so also worth 21 points); the two days of USAMO of year N serve as final TST worth 42 points. The sum across these five tests (six days, max 126 points) determines the IMO team. Notes: winning USAMO is neither necessary nor sufficient for IMO selection; selection spans a year; one cannot qualify for IMO without having attended MOP the previous year; team known shortly after USAMO grading in May.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taiwan IMO team selection procedure (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection via a sequence of tests/camps (APMOC → APMO → TST camps) with progressive cuts, mock IMOs and quizzes, and weights plus an oral interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For IMO 2014: high APMOC scores lead to a camp where APMO is given; top 30 on APMO invited to first TST camp; top 15 to second camp; top 10 to third camp. Each TST camp includes three Team Selection Quizzes (110 minutes, two olympiad problems) and a full mock IMO with six problems. Team decided by weighted sum of second & third TST camp scores plus an oral interview. Weighting roughly makes a mock IMO problem worth three quiz problems; overall selection takes a few months and is announced a few days into May. (Also notes: process may be updated and can include EGMO pathways.)

rubrics_metrics.name: USAMO/IMO per-problem grading rubric (7/6/5/2/1/0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Per-problem scores commonly use the USAMO rubric: 7 = problem solved; 6 = tiny slip (repairable); 5 = small non-central gap; 2 = lots of genuine progress; 1 = significant non-trivial progress; 0 = busy work/special cases/mostly irrelevant writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grading rewards complete solutions; typically solutions are classified as '7-' (has main ideas) or '0+' (missing a main idea). Scores 3 and 4 are often absent except in special two-part cases. Rubrics often do NOT use standard additive decomposition; e.g., two halves might be '2+2=7' or '3+5=7', and small partial observations might not sum in the 0+ case. 'Pocket change' around 7×complete_solutions can occur depending on rubric/captain. Graders don't give points for things they can't comprehend, and sympathy points are rare. Writing clearly reduces risk of misunderstanding. For examples, see USAMO 2003 rubric and USEMO reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: No regrades on USA(J)MO
rubrics_metrics.description: Regrade requests are not permitted for USA(J)MO/USAMO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AMC's long-standing policy: decisions of the USAMO graders are final and may not be appealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results/citations allowed without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: On USAMO/IMO, well-known results may be cited without full proof provided they do not trivialize the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no strict formal criteria; if unsure, include a brief sketch (a few sentences) of the proof rather than omitting it. See the English handout for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of detail required in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Include enough detail to convince the grader you understand the solution; avoid 'bluffing' with 'it's easy to see X' unless X is indeed trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is primarily a mathematical-clarity issue rather than style. The official solutions file for USAMO is about as terse as you can be; emulate that level of terseness but ensure the grader can follow the reasoning. When in doubt, write the short extra sentences to show understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for MOP invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: MOP invitations are not strictly defined but roughly include IMO team members, ~18 next non-graduating USAMO students, ~12 USAMO students in grades 9–10, ~12 top USAJMO students, and a varying number of non-graduating female contestants for EGMO representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact numbers/cutoffs vary year-to-year and are determined by scores for that year. Selection is done by ID number (not names). Consequence: one cannot attend MOP for the first time as a graduating 12th grader because the IMO selection process begins at the previous year's MOP. (Author's humorous aside about 8th graders.)

rubrics_metrics.name: MOP class/color assignment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: At MOP students are assigned to class tracks colloquially called Black, Blue, Green, Red based on performance/attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class assignments use USAMO score, TST rank, grade level, previous MOP attendance, and RMM/EGMO score. Invitations (who gets to attend MOP) are determined separately from class assignments. Color terminology is informal and not important for team selection; all USA students at MOP are treated equally in team selection regardless of color or past scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie-breaking on USA(J)MO
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy on when ties are broken is limited and has varied over years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between 2016–2019 ties were generally only broken for USAMO winners (because exactly 12 winners are invited to the state dinner). This did not happen in 2020–2021 (COVID). Starting in 2022 the USAMO switched to a different medal system. Practical implication: ties are not universally broken for ranking; specific procedures depend on the year.

rubrics_metrics.name: IMO coordination procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordination involves pre-set marking schemes and meetings between national leaders and problem coordinators to determine fair scores for each script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before the exam, marking schemes (rubrics) are prepared. Leaders see their country's students' solutions; host-country coordinators (and other coordinators) review scripts and meet with leaders to discuss scores. Leaders may translate non-English scripts. Leaders argue for their students (like defense attorneys); coordinators aim for uniform fairness (like prosecutors). In practice the process is collaborative — coordinators sometimes give higher scores than leaders, and leaders often try to show how partial solutions could be completed, especially for novel approaches. The goal is consistent, fair scoring across countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: IMO Shortlist (ISL) structure and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: The IMO Shortlist is a confidential list (~30 problems) from which six IMO problems are chosen; it's divided into Algebra, Combinatorics, Geometry, Number Theory and numbered roughly by difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shortlist typically has ~6–8 problems per category labeled A1,... C1,... etc., allowing references like '2011 G4'. Shortlisted problems are confidential for one year if they do not appear on IMO to protect problem security since many countries reuse shortlist problems for training and selection tests. The shortlist is selected from a larger 'longlist' (a few hundred proposed problems); modern selection is more competitive and non-selected longlist problems are often returned to authors for other use. Recent shortlists are indexed on AoPS and available on the official IMO website; early sharing/leaks should be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and attribution for contest problems/solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects expression, not ideas; attribute generously and avoid posting others' solutions verbatim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a non-legal overview (US-focused). If using problems/solutions not by you, attribute to avoid plagiarism. Changing wording can reduce copyright concerns but may not avoid plagiarism if you pass off problems as your own. Quoting a past USAMO problem on a public blog before giving your solution likely falls under fair use, but copying entire solutions verbatim is discouraged; better to cite the original author and rewrite the solution in your own words. Plagiarism may have institutional consequences even if not directly illegal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative difficulty of AIME I vs AIME II
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no systematic difference between AIME I and AIME II; the two drafts are randomly assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafts (given working names) are randomly assigned to I/II, so any perceived trends are noise. Corollary: grade level does not deterministically dictate class placement (e.g., 11th graders getting Red/Green is common). Practical implication: don't assume one version is easier or that grade restricts placement.
